**Key design decisions** (all stdlib-only, Python ≥3.11, pytest, interface exactly as specified):

- **One-time reads**: `os.unlink` of the record is the claim — POSIX guarantees exactly one concurrent caller succeeds, so FR-049's at-most-once falls out of the kernel with no lock, index, or tombstone. Content is read into memory *before* the claim (no partial bodies) and the claim runs *after* the password check (a 403 costs nothing).
- **Passwords**: per-paste 16-byte salt + `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", …, 200_000)` (~40 ms measured), compared with `secrets.compare_digest`. scrypt was the cryptographically stronger candidate but depends on an OpenSSL build flag and costs ~16 MB per concurrent check, so it was rejected to keep the zero-dependency promise unconditional.
- **Compatibility**: `RECORD_VERSION` stays `1` with the three new keys optional on read. Bumping it would make the existing reader report-and-skip every pre-upgrade paste — the exact failure FR-058/SC-017 forbid.
- **Ordering**: existence/expiry → password → claim → serve, documented as contractual in both the contract and the data model.
- **Scope**: two files change (`storage.py`, `server.py`), no new module, no new route; three new test modules so "the existing suite passes unmodified" stays literally checkable — `conftest.py` gets only additive helpers.

One judgment call worth flagging: KDF parameters live as module constants rather than per-record fields (Principle IV forbids the speculative discriminator). The consequence is written into research.md — changing the iteration count later would invalidate existing protected pastes and require a record-version bump.
